cards.text: This is a Psalm of David, and he's praying to the LORD. First words out of his mouth: 'O LORD, hear my prayer.' No small talk, no 'hope You're doing well.' He asks God to answer him in His faithfulness and His righteousness.
Then David asks God not to bring him into judgment. Friend, if anybody had inspected my first stamps in the Millers' kitchen, I'd have asked for the SAME thing.

cards.question: David asks God not to bring him into judgment. What reason does he give?

answers.text: No one alive is righteous before God
He has never done anything wrong
His enemies should be judged first

cards.text: Then David tells God what's going on. An enemy has been chasing him down, crushing his life to the ground.

cards.question: David says the enemy makes him dwell in darkness. He's like whom?
Inside, David says his spirit grows ___ and his heart is dismayed.

cards.text: But here the psalm turns. David's down, so he does what we all do on a rough day: he scrolls WAY back through the old photos. He remembers the days of old.

cards.question: When David looks back on the days of old, what does he think about?

cards.text: Then David stretches out his hands to God. Not a wave, friend. A REACH. Trust me, I know a reach when I see one. I raised six cookie cutters.

cards.question: David says his soul thirsts for God like a parched land.

cards.text: Then David hits the gas: 'Answer me quickly, O LORD; my spirit fails.' Not 'whenever You get a minute.' Not 'let's circle back Monday.' QUICKLY.

cards.question: David asks God not to hide His face from him. If God does, what does David say he'll be like?

answers.text: Those who descend to the Pit

cards.text: Then David asks for a wake-up call: 'Let me hear Your loving devotion in the morning, for I have put my trust in You.' Now THAT'S an alarm nobody's hitting snooze on.

cards.question: Next, David asks God to teach him how to defeat his enemies.
David asks the LORD to deliver him from his enemies. He says he flees to the ___ for refuge.

cards.text: Then comes the line this psalm is named for: 'Teach me to do Your will, for You are my God.' Honestly, friend? That's my prayer every morning before the first tray goes in. And again after it comes out.

cards.question: David asks God's good Spirit to lead him on level ground.
David asks the LORD to revive him and bring his soul out of trouble. For whose sake does he ask?

answers.text: For the sake of God's name
For the sake of his family
For the sake of his army

cards.question: In the last line, David asks God to cut off his ___ and calls himself God's ___.

findings.problem: The opening card runs four sentences: 'This is a Psalm of David…', 'First words out of his mouth…', 'No small talk…' and 'He asks God to answer him…'.

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: The joke adds something new to Papa Dorin's backstory. It says his first stamps in the Millers' kitchen would not have passed inspection. The backstory describes him arriving from a closing bakery and then 'years of good baking' with the Millers. It says nothing about weak early stamps, and the Millers' kitchen is not his bakery.

rule.text: His own world isn't Bible fact. His backstory, family, bakery and mission are the Dorinverse story in this file. He can talk about them freely, but never adds anything new to them. His jokes can make up small moments and habits around his bakery.

findings.problem: 'David's down, so he does…' adds a reason the text doesn't give. Verses 4 and 5 sit side by side. The text never says David remembers the days of old because he is down.

rule.text: Reasons: He never adds why someone did, said or thought something unless the text says why.

findings.problem: The joke puts the modern comparison inside the Bible scene: David himself 'scrolls WAY back through the old photos.' The comparison should stand apart from the Bible setting.

rule.text: One image only. Never blend the comparison with the Bible setting.

findings.problem: The story card has three sentences: 'But here the psalm turns.', 'David's down, so he does… old photos.' and 'He remembers the days of old.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The story card runs five sentences: 'Then David stretches…', 'Not a wave, friend.', 'A REACH.', 'Trust me, I know a reach…' and 'I raised six cookie cutters.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The punchline 'I know a reach when I see one. I raised six cookie cutters' doesn't connect. Nothing explains why raising cookie cutters would teach him what a reach looks like, so a stranger would say 'huh?'

rule.text: If a stranger would say "huh?", rewrite it.

findings.problem: The story card runs four sentences: the quote, 'Not whenever You get a minute.', 'Not let's circle back Monday.' and 'QUICKLY.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: Verse 8b is only tested with a false statement ('teach him how to defeat his enemies'). No card ever tells what David actually asks: 'Teach me the way I should walk, for to You I lift up my soul.' The baker leaves without that detail.

rule.text: When the baker leaves Prep, they understand the whole passage without missing an important detail.

findings.problem: The story card runs four sentences: the line about the psalm's name with the quote, 'Honestly, friend?', 'That's my prayer every morning…' and 'And again after it comes out.'

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: The card says 'David asks God's good Spirit to lead him.' In the text, David is speaking to God and says 'May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground.' He is not making a request addressed to the Spirit. This is the same pattern as the Naomi example in the rules.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them. ❌ "Naomi asks the LORD to bless them." ✅ "Naomi tells them, 'May the LORD…'" (Ruth 1:8)

findings.problem: Papa Dorin calls verse 10 'the line this psalm is named for.' The psalm's own heading in the text is 'A Psalm of David.' 'Teach Me to Do Your Will' is the passage title the lesson uses. That may count as talking about how lessons are made, and it may not be true of the psalm itself.
findings.question: May Papa Dorin refer to the passage title, for example by saying the psalm is 'named for' a line, or should he only refer to headings that appear in the BSB text itself?
